## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sūkarajātaka* (Ja 153), translated as *The Boar*, is a short canonical birth story preserved in the *Jātaka* section of the Khuddaka Nikāya. The canonical verse opens with the incipit *Catuppado ’haṁ samma* ("You are a fourfoot") [Fausböll 1879]. According to the narrative framework (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha related this discourse while residing at Jetavana near Sāvatthī, prompted by an aged elder (*aññataraṁ mahallakattheraṁ*) [Fausböll 1879].

In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), an insolent boar challenges a lion to combat, only to cover himself in filth; when the lion disdains fighting him, the boars flee in fear that the lion will return to destroy them [Fausböll 1879]. In the formal identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the Buddha reveals that the aged boar was the elderly monk of the present day, while the noble lion was the Buddha himself in a previous life [Fausböll 1879].
